title: Nsf Ach Fee: What It Costs and How to Avoid It
summary: Learn what an NSF ACH fee costs in 2026, how returned ACH debits differ from overdrafts, and practical steps to avoid NSF ACH fee charges.
body_markdown:
Say your account holds **$95** and a **$120** electric bill debit arrives. One bank returns it, charges a **$30** NSF fee, and your utility still needs paying. Another bank pays it, your balance drops to negative **$25** , and an overdraft fee applies instead. Neither outcome is automatic. You can review how[banking and payments rules interact](https://joingerald.com/learn/banking--payments) before your next debit date, but your own bank's policy decides which path your account takes.


The biller's fee sits on top of either outcome. Under Nacha rules described in a[Mayer Brown summary of the CFPB fee proposal](https://www.mayerbrown.com/en/insights/publications/2024/02/cfpb-proposes-latest-rule-in-initiative-against-socalled-junk-fees) , an originator may send a separate return fee entry only when permitted by applicable law, only for an **R01 or R09** return, after specific prior notice, and **only once per returned entry** , labeled **"RETURN FEE"** . So in the utility example, the utility can't add its own fee unless it gave notice and the law allows it.


### How common this is, and where it's heading


These fees rarely hit in isolation. The[CFPB report on overdraft and NSF practices](https://files.consumerfinance.gov/f/documents/cfpb_overdraft-nsf-report_2023-12.pdf) found that **26.5%** of consumers lived in households charged an overdraft or NSF fee during the prior year, **20.0%** experienced NSF fees specifically, and among consumers charged an NSF fee, **85%** were also charged an overdraft fee. That overlap points to a cash timing problem in the account, not a one-off penalty.


Exposure is shrinking, though. The[Consumer Financial Protection Bureau trend report on overdraft and NSF revenue](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/data-research/research-reports/trends-in-overdraftnon-sufficient-fund-nsf-fee-revenue-and-practices/) reported that overdraft and NSF-fee revenue fell by **more than 50% in 2023** compared with pre-pandemic levels, saving consumers **more than $6 billion annually** .


No NSF fee on your account doesn't mean no cost. Opting out of overdraft coverage can still leave a returned ACH, a biller fee, a late charge, or interrupted service.


That's the comparison worth making. A returned payment avoids a negative balance but leaves the bill unpaid and exposed to the biller's consequences. A paid payment keeps service running but puts you in the hole before the next deposit arrives.


## ACH Return Codes and How Re-presentment Adds Charges


When a bank returns an ACH debit, it attaches a **return code** explaining why. The[Increase documentation on ACH returns](https://increase.com/documentation/ach-returns) notes the ACH network identifies insufficient funds with return code **R01** , while **R09** denotes uncollected funds. That distinction matters because only certain codes can be tried again, and each new attempt can produce a new fee.


**R01** is the standard **NSF ACH fee** case. Your available balance couldn't cover the debit. **R09** is subtler. Money appears in the account, but the deposit hasn't cleared, so the bank won't release it. A debit timed against a paycheck that hasn't settled is a classic R09 setup.
